_note: Rolled per room after room types are assigned. requires[] filters on room tags. A rule with a `fixture` block builds an object that is not an item — a chest, a door, a body, a scatter of coins — and the block is where its vocabulary lives, so adding one never means touching the engine.

npc._note: An NPC rolls a role, two traits and a want. The persona string is assembled from them; the Narrator writes the voice.

guarantees._note: Applied after rolling, so an area is never barren or unlit. Not optional: small areas roll below expectation often enough that this pass is load-bearing.
guarantees._lightNote: Q6=B: no guarantee. Dark areas are a supply problem you solve before entering.
guarantees._slackNote: Roughly a third of rooms should hold nothing mechanical — that is where atmosphere lives. The cap stops a top-up filling a small area with fights.

wealth._note: An area's whole worth, budgeted rather than rolled room by room. Independent per-room rolls have no ceiling: a run of lucky chances put something valuable in every room, and one unlucky chest roll could produce a masterwork heirloom plate worth more than the rest of the world put together. So containers are counted, their contents are drawn from a value band rather than the whole item table, and coin is one purse for the area rather than a fresh roll per pile.
wealth._containerNote: Chests, corpses and anything else whose fixture sets the container flag, counted together. This is the gamified part: a container is a known number of chances at something good, so finding one means something. The low end is a floor topped up the same way hostiles and loot rooms are.

bands._note: priceRange filters which item bases may be drawn, in base gold BEFORE quality and affixes. Those still multiply on top — a masterwork heirloom is roughly 27x its base — so a band sets what kind of thing is found, not a hard cap on what it ends up worth. That is deliberate: the point of a chest is that it might hold something remarkable. The cap that matters is the number of containers, not the ceiling on any one of them. qualityBias replaces the loot tier's own bias for the roll, so a high band is both a better thing and a better example of it.

bandByTier._note: Weights per container, by the tier the room fights at. Ultra climbs with difficulty and is never quite zero — the deep room that might hold the good thing is the reason to walk into it.

wealth._looseNote: Items lying about a room are pinned to the low band so containers are where value lives. A room can still be worth searching; it is not worth looting.
wealth._deadEndNote: A container at the end of a branch (not a through-room, not the entry) rolls its band as if the room were this many tiers higher. Depth already prices in danger via the room's own tier; this is reward following position on top of that, so a side trail's promise is real rather than a coin flip.

goldBudgetByTier._note: One purse for the whole area, spent down by gold piles and by any purse that rolls as loot. When it runs out, later coin is whatever is left, and a spill with nothing behind it is simply not made.
